[16-24] Pharaoh is deeply pleased by the arrival of Joseph's brothers and supports the plan to bring Jacob, ordering that wagons be provided for the families' transport and urging them not to cling to their temporary possessions, since the best of all the land of Egypt would be theirs. When provisions are distributed, Benjamin is given three hundred pieces of silver and five sets of clothing, which again links him to the number five, typologically associated with death in Scripture.
[25-28] The brothers return to Canaan and announce to their elderly father that Joseph is alive and ruling over all Egypt. Jacob's heart initially melts with disbelief upon receiving such overwhelming news after twenty-two years of uninterrupted mourning. However, upon hearing all his son's words and, particularly, upon seeing the chariots and goods that he had sent from the Egyptian court, Jacob's spirit revived. It is noteworthy to observe that his spiritual reactivation stemmed from walking by sight and not by absolute faith, finding comfort in contemplating the material provisions, the food, and the transport.

[1-4] Jacob seeks God first and offers sacrifices before making his final plans to descend to Egypt. In the night visions, God calls him by name twice, a pattern of divine calling that is repeated with other biblical figures throughout Scripture. Unlike Abraham and Isaac, for whom the descent to Egypt brought severe hardship (Genesis 12; Genesis 26), Jacob receives explicit divine approval and the promise: “I will go down with you to Egypt.” This promise establishes the spiritual principle that the believer is safe in the world as long as the Lord remains with him (1 John 4:4). The phrase "Joseph will lay his hand on your eyes" indicates the promise that his beloved son would be at his bedside to gently close his eyes at the moment of his death.
[5-7] Jacob descends to Egypt with all his descendants, thus fulfilling the prophecy previously given to Abraham that his descendants would be foreigners and afflicted in a foreign land (Genesis 15:13).
[8-27] The extensive genealogical list presents apparent numerical discrepancies that are resolved congruently upon careful examination of the details of the text. The passage mentions sixty-six people, then seventy, and later in the New Testament, seventy-five are mentioned (Acts 7:14). The number sixty-six refers exclusively to the souls who came from Jacob's loins and physically entered Egypt with him on that journey, excluding Er and Onan, who had already died in Canaan, as well as Joseph, Ephraim, and Manasseh, who were already residing in Egyptian territory. The number seventy is reached by adding Jacob, Joseph, and Joseph's two sons to the previous group. The figure of seventy-five, cited by the martyr Stephen, includes the wives of Jacob's sons and other relatives who complete "all his kindred." Additionally, the record emphasizes the primary genealogical order rather than the chronological rigor of the exact moment of the journey, which is why it includes Judah's grandsons (Hezron and Hamul), who must have been born later in Egypt. [28-30] Judah is sent ahead as a forerunner to Goshen, whose name means "to approach." Jacob's physical reunion with Joseph, after more than two decades of uninterrupted mourning, is typologically similar to Job's final restoration (Job 42:10). This event foreshadows the condition of the nation of Israel at the end of the Tribulation, when its profound historical losses are finally restored by divine grace. Satisfied and comforted, Jacob declares himself ready to die now that he has verified that his son is still alive. [31-34] Joseph strategically instructs his brothers to declare to Pharaoh that their occupation is shepherding, forewarning the cultural reality that "the Egyptians detest all shepherds." This strong abhorrence was not solely due to social prejudices or historical resentments toward invading kings, but to a profound religious clash: the Hebrews sacrificed sheep and showed no reverence for cows, which the Egyptians venerated as sacred. In essence, the idolatrous Egyptian could not tolerate the blood of the lamb. Since Egypt consistently operates as a type of the world system throughout Scripture, this passage illustrates the perpetual enmity the world professes toward the Good Shepherd (John 10:1-28) and toward the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

[1-6] Joseph presents five of his brothers to Pharaoh. The number five figures prominently in Joseph’s ministry throughout this narrative (Genesis 47:2, 24). The brothers are granted permission to live in the land of Goshen, and the Egyptian monarch demonstrates such confidence in Joseph’s administration that he asks him to appoint capable men from among his brothers to oversee his own livestock. This governmental provision proves providential for the patriarchal family, since the pastures in Canaan had been unproductive during two years of famine. [7-10] Jacob is presented to Pharaoh. Instead of adopting a servile posture or attempting to buy favors, the patriarch assumes his prophetic role before the Gentile ruler and blesses him directly (Genesis 47:10). His statement that the days of his wandering have been "few and evil" (Genesis 47:9) accurately reflects the harsh reality of the consequences of his past deceptions and family conflicts. At 130 years old, his longevity had not yet reached that of his ancestors, since Isaac lived 180 years and Abraham 175. Eventually, Jacob would live 17 years in Egypt and die at the age of 147 (Genesis 47:28).
[18-26] During the fifth and sixth years of the famine, the population is forced into a state of absolute state dependency, where the government assumes formal control of the land and the bodies of its citizens to preserve them from starvation (Genesis 47:19-20). This condition, in which the inhabitants surrender their possessions to the supreme leader for sustenance, foreshadows the earthly circumstances of absolute governmental control that will prevail during the Tribulation period (Revelation 13:16-17). The fifth, or 20 percent, tax established by Joseph as an agrarian statute (Genesis 47:24) is not a tyrannical slave tax, but a fair administrative arrangement that allowed farming families to subsist through the provision of seeds. The command to move the people to the cities (Genesis 47:21) was logistically intended to concentrate the population near granaries and food distribution centers, not to subject them to oppressive slavery, contrary to textual alterations in manuscripts such as the Septuagint that erroneously suggest Joseph made them captive servants. [27-31] Israel dwells in Goshen and multiplies greatly (Genesis 47:27). As the time of his death drew near, Jacob required Joseph to swear a solemn oath not to bury him in Egypt, but in the land of his fathers in Canaan, demonstrating his continued faith in the covenant promise concerning the land (Genesis 47:29-30). This procedure under oath is similar to the one Abraham had previously required of his servant Eliezer. Verse 31 states that Israel bowed down in worship at the head of his bed. Historically, Alexandrian scribes altered this passage in the Septuagint translation to force an artificial concordance with the reading of Hebrews 11:21, changing the term "bed" to "staff," a mistranslation later used doctrinally by Catholicism to attempt to justify the veneration of images through inanimate objects. In correct biblical hermeneutics, the events of Genesis 47:31 and Hebrews 11:21 are entirely distinct incidents; The worship leaning on the end of his staff mentioned in Hebrews corresponds to a chronologically later moment, precisely when Jacob prophetically blesses Joseph's two sons (Genesis 48:1-14).

[1-7] The narrative describes Jacob as ill, receiving a visit from Joseph and his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob struggles to sit up in bed and recalls the divine appearance at Luzah, referring to the Creator as "God Almighty" or El Shaddai. In an act of profound legal and prophetic significance, the patriarch claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, equating them in status with Reuben and Simeon. This action constitutes the transfer of the double portion of the birthright to the line of Joseph (1 Chronicles 5:1-2), replacing Reuben and Simeon because of the grave sins the latter had previously committed (Genesis 34:25; Genesis 35:22).
[8-12] With his eyesight clouded by old age, Israel inquires about the identity of the young men, who by this time would have been around twenty-five or twenty-six years old. As they approach, Jacob kisses and embraces them, in a scene that echoes the actions his own father, Isaac, performed decades earlier when imparting the blessing (Genesis 27:22, 27). When Joseph removes them from between his knees, Jacob leans forward on his staff with his face to the ground and worships (Hebrews 11:21; Genesis 48:12). The text establishes that it is in this exact context, and not before, that the staff-leaning worship mentioned in the New Testament occurs, refuting the alterations of corrupted manuscripts that attempt to place this act in Genesis 47:31. [13-20] Joseph arranges the young men so that Manasseh, the firstborn, is on Israel's right hand, and Ephraim, the youngest, on his left. However, the patriarch deliberately crosses his hands. By blessing them, he acknowledges that the Lord has fulfilled the part of the covenant he himself had conditioned years before (Genesis 28:20) and mentions the "angel who keeps me safe from all harm," presenting a figure closely related to that of a guardian angel (Revelation 1:20). Joseph is displeased to see his hands folded and tries to correct his father, but Jacob refuses, prophetically stating that although Manasseh will be a great nation, his younger brother will be greater than he. Historically, Ephraim's preeminence over Manasseh is verified in the first desert census (Numbers 1:33, 35), and over the centuries, the name Ephraim came to be used synonymously to represent the ten northern tribes during their times of apostasy (Hosea 4:17; Hosea 5:9).
[21-22] In his final statement of the chapter, Israel assures Joseph that God will bring them back to the land of their fathers, a promise based on the oral revelation passed down from Abraham (Genesis 15:14). Finally, Jacob grants Joseph an additional "portion" over his brothers, acquired with his "sword" and his "bow." The Hebrew term used here for portion is "Shekem," which literally translates as "shoulder," and is used in Scripture to refer to war booty carried on the shoulders. This portion should not be confused with territorial possession, nor with the city of Shechem, nor with the peaceful event of the purchase of the field (Genesis 33:19), much less with the massacre perpetrated by Simeon and Levi from which Jacob completely disassociated himself (Genesis 34; Genesis 49:5-6). None of Jacob's descendants would receive portions of land until two hundred and fifteen years later, under the leadership of Joshua. The true inheritance of the believer in his earthly pilgrimage is an "incorruptible inheritance" that does not fade away (1 Peter 1:4).

[1-2] On his deathbed, the patriarch outlines the details of prophetic history more than 3,600 years in advance. The chapter covers the two comings of Jesus Christ, the figure of the Antichrist, the future of the twelve tribes of Israel, and the designation of the tribe that will hold royal dominion.
[3-4] Reuben, being the firstborn, was destined to be the strength, the beginning of vigor, and the excellence of Israel. However, because of his sin of incest (Genesis 35:22), he irrevocably loses the material, priestly, and royal blessings, which pass to Joseph, Levi, and Judah, respectively. The phrase "unstable as water" accurately describes his weakness of character and subsequent moral decline, illustrating the inescapable principle of sowing and reaping. [5-7] Simeon and Levi receive a severe rebuke. The "weapons of iniquity" refer directly to the swords used in the vengeful massacre of Shechem (Genesis 34:25), a crime from which Jacob completely absolves himself and disassociates himself. The action described as tearing down a wall indicates an aggressive act of violence against property, in contrast to the alterations of corrupt texts that erroneously suggest they hamstrung oxen (Genesis 34:28-29). As divine judgment, both tribes suffer dispersion; Simeon becomes the smallest tribe of Israel, and Levi is scattered throughout the nation without a continuous inheritance of his own. [8-10] The preeminence and monarchical honors fall sovereignly upon Judah, establishing the lineage from which the true King of the Kingdom of Heaven will come. Judah is exalted to this position of leadership after having humbled himself on previous occasions, taking his own guilt (Genesis 38:26) and offering himself as a substitute for his brother (Genesis 44:18-34). The prophecy guarantees that the scepter and the lawgiver will not depart from Judah until "Shiloh" (the Peaceful One) comes, securing the tribe's authority until the coming of the Messiah. [11] The two comings of Jesus Christ are condensed into a single verse, separated only by a punctuation mark. Tying the donkey to the vine foreshadows the Triumphal Entry during his first earthly coming (Matthew 21:4-11). Immediately afterward, the image of washing his garments in the wine and blood of the grapes prophetically points to his second coming, when the Messiah will tread the winepress of God's wrath and his garments will be stained with the blood of his enemies in the eschatological conflict (Isaiah 63:1-4; Revelation 14:18-20, 19:13).
[13] Zebulun's territorial portion extends from Galilee to the ports of Phoenicia, literally fulfilling the declaration that it would be a "port of ships" and would dwell on the shores of the sea.
[16-17] Extremely grim prophecies surround the future of the tribe of Dan. He is compared to a poisonous snake on the road that bites the heels of horses, typologically linking this tribe with Satan and the Antichrist (Genesis 3:15). Historically, Dan is the first tribe to fall fully into apostasy and systematic idolatry, and in the coming Tribulation period, it is not included in the list of tribes sealed for divine protection (Revelation 7).
[18] The exclamation "I have waited for your salvation, O Lord" (King James Version) places the speaker doctrinally and eschatologically at the end of the Great Tribulation period, awaiting the ultimate deliverance that comes with the visible return of the Lord (Matthew 24:13).
[22-26] Multiple and extensive blessings are heaped upon the head of Joseph, who is described as a fruitful bough by a spring. In its spiritual application, it represents the believer who remains in Christ and bears unceasing fruit despite being hated and attacked by the "archers" (a figure of persecution that also prophetically points to the events of the Tribulation). In verse 24, another separation of the two advents is observed by means of a typological comma: the "shepherd" is mentioned (referring to the first advent, John 10:11), as well as the "rock of Israel" (referring to the second advent, the stone that crushes the nations in Daniel 2:34, 45). Joseph is exalted and crowned with blessings of heaven and earth because he previously took the place of a servant, resisted temptation, forgave his brothers from the heart, and ruled without oppressing the people. [33] Having completed his prophetic instructions, Jacob draws his feet up into the bed and dies. The text accurately states that "he was gathered to his people" at the time of his departure, an event that occurs at least seventy days before his physical body is laid in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 50:3). This temporal sequence conclusively demonstrates the biblical doctrine that the soul separates and has an immediate conscious destiny before the physical body is buried, refuting notions that erroneously equate the grave with the final abode of the soul.

[1-3] Joseph weeps and kisses the face of his deceased father. Egyptian physicians embalm Israel, a process that took forty days and historically included the removal of organs and the use of spices to preserve the physical body. The book of Genesis, which begins gloriously with the Creator of life, moves toward its conclusion with the inescapable reminder of God's judgment on sin, where the flesh returns to the dust of the earth. [4-6] Joseph recounts the oath he swore to his father and asks Pharaoh for permission to go and bury him. The mention of the term "grave" in verse 5 refers exclusively to a hole dug in the ground or a niche in a cave (from the Hebrew word "keberi"), and has no connection whatsoever with Sheol or Hades. This maintains the doctrinal precision of the biblical text, clearly separating the temporal destiny of the physical body from the conscious destiny and dwelling place of the soul. [7-14] A vast funeral procession leaves Egypt for Canaan. Unlike the nation's future exodus under Moses' leadership, on this occasion the Israelites leave the children and flocks in the land of Goshen. They arrive at the threshing floor of Atad, where the mourning is so profound and evident that the Canaanites observe the scene and name the place Abel-mizraim. Finally, Jacob's sons fulfill his instructions by burying him in the cave in the field of Machpelah, the same place Abraham had acquired for his family. [15-18] After the funeral and on their return to Egypt, guilt resurfaces in the consciences of Joseph's brothers. They fear that, now that Jacob's protective influence is gone, Joseph will seek revenge for the wrong they did to him decades ago. They send a message claiming that Jacob, before dying, asked Joseph to forgive his brothers' transgression. However, Joseph's reaction—weeping upon hearing this—shows that he had already forgiven the offense from the heart long before and harbored no resentment that needed to be appeased. The brothers then prostrate themselves before him, offering themselves willingly as his servants. [19-21] Joseph comforts them with the words, "Do not be afraid: Am I in the place of God?" He then practically articulates the theological principle that is later codified in the New Testament. This passage irrefutably demonstrates how the anger and wicked schemes of men are used by divine sovereignty to accomplish redemptive purposes, foreshadowing exactly how the evil perpetrated against Jesus Christ at Calvary culminated in the salvation of humanity (Acts 2:23; Romans 8:28). In his forgiving attitude, Joseph comforts and speaks kindly to his people, foreshadowing Jesus Christ restoring his own. [22-26] Joseph lives to the age of one hundred and ten and sees the third generation of his descendants. Before he dies, he makes the children of Israel swear that they will carry his bones out of Egypt at the time of God's visitation, a promise of faith (Hebrews 11:22) that is faithfully fulfilled under Moses (Exodus 13:19). Typologically, Egypt represents the system of this world. Just as Joseph's bones were taken out of there, the bones of Jesus Christ did not remain in the earthly tomb of this world, but ascended to heaven (Luke 24:39, 51). In the same way, the born-again believer expects to be taken from this temporary world in the resurrection and rapture to be with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16-18). The revelation of the first book of the Bible culminates somberly with the phrase "and was placed in an ark in Egypt," firmly establishing that, without the book of Exodus and the subsequent work of redemption, the natural destiny of fallen man is eternally limited to death and the grave.
